title: Coral and the Gravity
premise: Oscar Dravenmoor, navigator of the freighter Coral and the Gravity, has spent three years hauling cargo through contested orbits while hiding the ship's darkest secret: a hold full of illegal consciousness backups, including one of himself. When the warship Meridian returns from deep space with its entire crew aged backward into children, Oscar is the only navigator who can read its impossible flight logs — and the only witness to what the backups were really for. Hunted by both warring factions, he must carry a message recovered from the Meridian's core to a neutral relay station, discovering along the way that the war itself was engineered to force humanity into mass backup-immortality. In the end, Oscar chooses to broadcast the truth and destroy his own backup, ending the war by making immortality impossible — and finally belonging, briefly and mortally, to the living crew around him.
about_author: Ada Ashgrove is a former orbital logistics analyst who spent a decade writing shipping manifests before turning them into fiction. She lives near a decommissioned launch site and writes about people who keep things running.

chapters.title: Manifest Weight
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A routine cargo run through contested orbit establishes the Coral and the Gravity's crew and the quiet dread of the sealed hold where the backups sleep. Oscar lies to a customs drone and to himself. Emotional beat: numb routine masking guilt.

chapters.title: The Hold We Don't Open
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Engineer Sefa discovers Oscar's private backup among the crates — a version of him three years stale. Instead of reporting it, she asks why he's still afraid of it. Flashback to the accident that made him back himself up. Beat: shame surfacing.

chapters.title: Meridian
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A distress ping draws them to the warship Meridian drifting dead at the edge of contested space. Boarding, they find a full crew complement — all of them children, wearing adult uniforms, with no memory of aging forward or back. Beat: creeping horror.

chapters.title: Children of the Deep
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: ship's doctor Imara. The child-crew are physically seven but retain fragmented adult skills — a girl navigates by instinct, a boy disassembles a reactor. Imara realizes their cells are running time in reverse. Beat: wonder tangled with dread.

chapters.title: Flight Logs in Reverse
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Only Oscar can parse the Meridian's scrambled navigation data; the logs read backward, ending at a launch that hasn't happened. The final entry is a message addressed to whoever finds the ship. Beat: the hook tightens.

chapters.title: Two Flags, One Wreck
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. Both warring factions claim the Meridian. A Republic patrol and a Concordat cutter arrive simultaneously; the Coral escapes by threading a debris field only Oscar can fly. Beat: adrenaline, and the first taste of being hunted.

chapters.title: What the Message Says
chapters.summary: Oscar and Imara's POV, alternating. Decrypted, the message reveals the Meridian's mission: proof that the war's escalation was orchestrated by the Continuity Consortium, which profits from selling backup-immortality to a terrified population. Beat: the ground shifts under everything.

chapters.title: The Price of the Hold
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Captain Voss wants to sell the message to the Republic; Sefa wants it public; Imara warns it could ignite the war it was meant to end. Oscar realizes the backups in their own hold are Consortium product. Beat: complicity.

chapters.title: Port of Small Mercies
chapters.summary: Imara's POV. Resupply at the neutral station Halcyon Reach. The child-crew, temporarily aboard, experience kindness — a market, a dog, rain recycled from a dome. Beat: tenderness, and what they stand to lose.

chapters.title: Republic Hands
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A Republic admiral offers Oscar amnesty, a clean record, and a new identity — in exchange for the message and silence about the Consortium. The offer is everything Oscar has wanted for three years. Beat: temptation.

chapters.title: Concordat Knives
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. Concordat agents board under diplomatic cover and try to seize the children as evidence. Voss is shot covering the escape; the Coral flees damaged. Beat: loyalty tested with blood.

chapters.title: Voss's Ledger
chapters.summary: Voss's POV, dying. She confesses she's known about the Consortium for a decade and took their money — the Coral's charter was always a laundering route. She gives Oscar her access codes and her blessing to do better. Beat: grief and absolution.

chapters.title: The Stale Copy
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Cornered and doubting, Oscar nearly restores his three-year-old backup to pilot the damaged ship through a gravity well. Sefa talks him out of it: the man in the hold doesn't know what Oscar knows now. Beat: identity as choice, not data.

chapters.title: Halcyon Burns
chapters.summary: Imara's POV. The Republic, then the Concordat, bombard the neutral station to destroy the Meridian's surviving records. The Coral rescues survivors — including the admiral who tried to buy Oscar. Beat: both sides are the same fire.

chapters.title: Time Runs Out
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The child-navigator's reverse-aging is accelerating; Imara calculates she'll reach birth within weeks. The message must be broadcast from the Meridian's original launch point in deep space — a six-week jump they must make in four. Beat: the clock becomes the antagonist.

chapters.title: Threading the Well
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The desperate run through a collapsing gravity well, Oscar flying on instinct and the dying child's backward memories guiding him. They arrive with the ship breaking apart. Beat: sacrifice of machine and self.

chapters.title: The Consortium's Face
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. At the launch point they find the Consortium's archive station — and a reception committee led by the man whose signature is on every backup crate, including Oscar's. He offers Oscar his original body's continuation: restore the backup, live forever, forget all of this. Beat: the final temptation, power offered gently.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV, interwoven. Oscar transmits the message on every open channel: the war manufactured, the immortality trade built on it, the Meridian's children as proof of what the technology really does. Both fleets receive it mid-battle. Beat: the truth as detonation.

chapters.title: What the Fleets Do
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. Instead of ending, the war nearly ignites — until the child-navigator, now days from birth, broadcasts her own backward memories fleet-wide. Soldiers see the future their masters built. Ceasefires ripple outward. Beat: catharsis through the smallest witness.

chapters.title: Deleting Oscar Dravenmoor
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. In the hold, Oscar deletes his own backup — and every other one aboard — choosing mortality and the people in front of him over the man he was. The hold goes dark and stays dark. Beat: the theme made flesh; grief and relief.

chapters.title: Gravity
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The armistice holds at Halcyon Reach, half-ruined and rebuilding. The child-navigator is born, and Imara holds her. Oscar takes a honest contract, a small one. Beat: belonging, earned and temporary.

chapters.title: Coral
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV, closing. The Coral and the Gravity, patched and repainted, makes its first postwar run with a crew who chose each other. Sefa opens the old hold and finds it just a hold. Final line lands on the living, moving forward. Beat: quiet, durable hope.
